pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: What does `if r := n % 10; r == 0` do, step by step? Where does `r` exist, and why is that a feature?
expected_points: the short statement runs first, then the condition is checked
r is scoped to the if (and its else) only — gone after the closing brace
keeps single-decision helpers from leaking into the surrounding function

questions.prompt: When do you reach for `switch` instead of an if/else chain, and what happens at the end of a Go `case` compared to C?
expected_points: switch when comparing one value against fixed candidates; condition-less switch tidies long else-if chains
Go breaks implicitly — a finished case ends the whole switch
fallthrough exists but must be written explicitly and is rare

questions.prompt: Go has one loop keyword. Describe the four shapes of `for` and give a situation where each fits.
expected_points: classic init; condition; post — counting with a known range
condition-only — a while loop: repeat until something changes
bare for — infinite loop exited by break/return: wait-until-done work
range — do something n times / walk each element; over an int it yields 0..n-1

questions.prompt: In nested loops, what exactly do plain `continue`, plain `break`, and `continue outer` (with a label) each skip?
expected_points: continue abandons the current iteration of the innermost loop; the post statement still runs
break exits the innermost loop entirely
a labeled continue/break acts on the named (outer) loop — e.g. rejecting a candidate from inside an inner divisor loop

questions.prompt: You write a `switch` inside a `for` and put `break` in one of its cases. What does that `break` actually exit, and how would you exit the loop instead?
expected_points: it breaks the switch, not the for loop
label the loop and use a labeled break (or restructure with a return/condition)

questions.prompt: What values does `for i := range 5` produce, and when would that difference from 1..5 bite you?
expected_points: fine when only counting iterations; bites when the counter's value is used, e.g. summing 1..n or printing positions
